turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth was quick to remind Mr. Darcy that she had seen him in a very different light long before Mr. Wickham’s account had come to her.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Mr Darcy was unprepared for such a direct challenge to his character, he told Elizabeth, and he wished to clarify the misunderstandings that had led to her unfavourable opinion of him.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth was taken aback by Mr Darcy’s sudden admission, yet she remained firm in her stance, telling Mr Darcy that his past actions had deeply affected her opinion of him.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: He felt compelled to address her concerns, telling Elizabeth that he had come to understand the error of his ways and that his pride had been his greatest obstacle.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth felt a mix of surprise and disbelief, telling Mr Darcy that though she was glad to hear of his supposed change of heart, it was difficult to see him as anything but the proud and prejudiced man she had always known.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: He felt compelled to explain further, telling Elizabeth that though his pride had indeed been a barrier, he had come to see the error in his ways and hoped to earn her regard through his actions going forward.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth crossed her arms, her tone sharp as she spoke to Mr Darcy, telling him that his past actions had not been merely a matter of pride but had caused real harm to those around him, including her family.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: He was acutely aware of the weight of his past actions, acknowledging to Elizabeth that her family had indeed suffered because of his pride and prejudice.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth was not convinced, she told Mr Darcy, that his change of heart would be enough to repair the damage he had caused, nor that it would be enough to earn her respect or affection.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: He was deeply affected by her words, acknowledging the hurt he had caused and expressing his sincere desire to make amends.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth told Mr Darcy that she was not yet ready to believe that his change of heart was genuine, and that actions would speak louder than words.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: He understood her doubt, acknowledging that his actions had earned her disdain and that he must prove himself through his deeds, not merely his words.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth was not yet ready to give in to Mr Darcy’s declaration, she told him, and would need to see substantial changes in his behavior before she could consider mending their relationship.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: He understood her reluctance and promised to work on himself, hoping to earn her respect and affection through his actions alone.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: She was not convinced by his words alone, Elizabeth told Mr Darcy, and would need to see a true transformation in his character before she could even consider his sentiments.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: He vowed to himself to change, telling Elizabeth that he would prove his sincerity through his actions.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Elizabeth was not easily swayed by promises, she told Mr Darcy, and would need to see a clear change in his behavior before she could believe in his sincerity.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: He was determined to prove her wrong, he declared, and would strive to alter his ways to earn her regard.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: She was not so easily persuaded, she told him, and would wait to see the fruits of his efforts before she could consider any change in her opinion.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: He was not accustomed to such direct challenges to his character, but he would not be deterred, he assured her, and would work diligently to earn her esteem.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy told Elizabeth that he had struggled in vain and that it would not do. His feelings would not be repressed, and he must allow him to tell her how ardently he admired and loved her.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth replied to Mr. Darcy that in such cases, it was believed to be the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It was natural that obligation should be felt, and if she could feel gratitude, she would now thank him. But she could not, for she had never desired his good opinion, and he had certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. She was sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone, but it had been most unconsciously done and she hoped it would be of short duration. The feelings which he told her had long prevented the acknowledgment of his regard could have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy told Elizabeth that this was all the reply which he was to have the honour of expecting. He might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, he was thus rejected. But it was of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth told Mr. Darcy that she might as well ask why, with such a clear intention of offending and insulting her, he chose to tell her that he liked her against his will, against his reason, and even against his character. Was not this some excuse for incivility, if she was uncivil? But she had other provocations. He knew she had. Had not her own feelings decided against him, had they been indifferent, or even favourable, did he think that any consideration would tempt her to accept the man who had been the means of ruining, perhaps forever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth told Mr. Darcy that she had every reason in the world to think ill of him. No motive could excuse the unjust and ungenerous part he had acted there. He dared not, he could not deny that he had been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth told Mr. Darcy that it was not merely this affair on which her dislike was founded. Long before it had taken place, her opinion of him was decided. His character was unfolded in the recital which she had received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what could he have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship could he here defend himself? Or under what misrepresentation could he here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy told Elizabeth that she took an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth replied to Mr. Darcy that who that knew what his misfortunes had been could help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy told Elizabeth that his misfortunes had indeed been great indeed.
